stages.note: The commands on this page are for a Linux or macOS terminal. On Windows, you run them in WSL2: a Linux system that Microsoft builds into Windows 10 (version 2004 or later) and Windows 11. On macOS or Linux, skip this stage.

steps.who: The agent opens an administrator PowerShell after your yes; Windows asks you to approve it (UAC)
steps.d: Check first (no change, no admin needed): Get-CimInstance Win32_OptionalFeature -Filter "Name='VirtualMachinePlatform'" and the same for Name='Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux' (InstallState 1 = enabled, 2 = disabled, 3 = absent). Check the Ubuntu distro too: no entries under HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Lxss means none installed. If both features are on, the feature step needs no restart: say so, and only the Ubuntu install is left. Only if a feature is off, after your yes, the agent starts an elevated PowerShell (Start-Process powershell -Verb RunAs) that runs the command and writes its output to a log file. You approve the Windows admin prompt on your screen. The install turns on the features WSL2 needs: they take effect after a restart, because Windows loads the WSL2 Linux kernel at boot. A failed install stops with the log's last lines; the agent does not retry in a loop. Restart only if a feature was off before the install, and only after you say yes; the agent saves the ledger first. After the restart, the agent checks again: if no Ubuntu with VERSION 2 is listed, it runs this install again after your yes.
steps.d_human: Open PowerShell as administrator (Windows asks you to approve it) and run the command. It turns on the Windows features WSL2 needs and installs Ubuntu. Restart Windows if the install asks for it. After the restart, run the command again if Ubuntu is missing from the output of wsl --list --verbose.

steps.d: After the install (and the restart, if one was needed), open Ubuntu from the Start menu once. The first start asks you to make a Linux user name and password; the agent cannot run commands in Ubuntu until you do this. Then say "done". Run every later command on this page in this Ubuntu window.
steps.d_human: After the install (and the restart, if one was needed), open Ubuntu from the Start menu once. The first start asks you to make a Linux user name and password. Run every later command on this page in this Ubuntu window. How to use the Ubuntu window: Open it from the Start menu (type Ubuntu), or type wsl in PowerShell. Paste with a right-click (Ctrl+V and Ctrl+Shift+V may print ^V and do nothing in this window). Copy by selecting the text with the mouse, then right-click or press Enter. Ctrl+C does NOT copy: it stops the running command. If the right-click paste fails: right-click the PowerShell title bar, Properties, Options, tick 'Use Ctrl+Shift+C/V as Copy/Paste', OK, then reopen the window; paste with Ctrl+Shift+V. Passwords do not show on screen while you type; that is normal. Press Enter after the password.
steps.c: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl unzip jq openssl ca-certificates

steps.d: Click the link in the verification email soon after you get it. If the link has expired, sign in at multicloud.io and ask for a new email. If no email arrives, check your spam or quarantine folder, then tell your Multicloud contact.
You become the organization owner. Write down the organization ID: you may need it later.

stages.note: An AI agent can run the commands on this page for you and explain each step. Any agent that can run terminal commands and use MCP servers works. Without an AI, run the commands yourself.

steps.h: Connect your AI tool to Multicloud
steps.d: Pick your AI tool below. Each one adds the Multicloud MCP server (https://mcp.multicloud.io/mcp, Streamable HTTP) and signs you in with your multicloud.io account in the browser. You need no key. Then ask your AI to list the Multicloud tools to check the connection.
steps.g: Restart your AI tool after the change if it does not show the Multicloud tools.

tools.label: Claude Code
tools.d: Run this in a terminal. Then, in Claude Code, run /mcp, select multicloud and sign in.
tools.c: claude mcp add --transport http --scope user multicloud https://mcp.multicloud.io/mcp

tools.label: Claude (desktop and web)
tools.d: Open Customize › Connectors › + Add › Add custom connector. Name: Multicloud. URL: the address below. Then click Connect and sign in. On a Team or Enterprise plan, an owner adds the connector in Organization settings › Connectors, and each member clicks Connect.

tools.label: Cursor
tools.d: Add this to ~/.cursor/mcp.json (all projects) or .cursor/mcp.json (one project). If the file has other servers, add only the multicloud entry. Cursor asks you to sign in the first time. Cursor CLI: cursor-agent mcp login multicloud.

tools.label: GitHub Copilot
tools.d: Add this to ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json (all projects) or .mcp.json in the workspace root. If the file has other servers, add only the multicloud entry. If Copilot does not open a sign-in, use an API key (last step of this stage) as the header Authorization: Bearer mca_…

tools.label: OpenAI Codex
tools.d: Run this in a terminal. The second command opens the browser to sign in.
tools.c:
codex mcp add multicloud --url https://mcp.multicloud.io/mcp
codex mcp login multicloud

tools.label: Gemini CLI
tools.d: Run this in a terminal. Then, in Gemini CLI, run /mcp auth multicloud and sign in.
tools.c: gemini mcp add --scope user --transport http multicloud https://mcp.multicloud.io/mcp

tools.label: Another AI tool
tools.d: Add a remote MCP server in your tool's MCP settings: URL https://mcp.multicloud.io/mcp, transport Streamable HTTP. Most tools open a browser to sign in. If yours cannot, use an API key (last step of this stage) as the header Authorization: Bearer mca_…. The block below is the common JSON form.

steps.h: Add the Multicloud onboarding skill (if your AI supports skills)
steps.d: Recommended. The multicloud-onboarding skill runs this whole page with you: it asks what you want to run, checks your computer, connects your AWS account, requests quota and runs the first workload. It asks before each change, and keeps a ledger so you can continue after a quota wait. Example for Claude Code (the skills are public at github.com/multicloud/skills):
steps.c:
claude plugin marketplace add multicloud/skills
claude plugin install multicloud-onboarding@multicloud
steps.g: Restart Claude Code after the install (claude --continue), then say: “Run the Multicloud GPU PoC”. To update: claude plugin marketplace update multicloud, then claude plugin update multicloud-onboarding@multicloud, then restart.

steps.h: Only if your AI tool cannot sign in: create an API key
steps.d: On multicloud.io, open Account › API keys and click Create. Copy the key now: the console shows it only once. Put it into your AI tool's MCP settings as the header Authorization: Bearer mca_… and nowhere else. Never paste it into a chat.

stages.t: Install the tools and sign in to AWS
stages.note: You need command-line tools. Your AI can install them for you, or you can run the commands below yourself. After the installs, close your Ubuntu window and open Ubuntu again from the Start menu. A window opened before the install cannot find aws, tofu, kubectl, helm, jq or mctl. Then check with: aws --version

steps.h: Optional: ask your AI to connect AWS
steps.d: Say: “Connect my AWS account to Multicloud. Use region us-east-1.” Your AI checks which tools are missing and guides you through this stage and the next one. The commands below are the same steps, if you prefer to run them yourself.
mctl needs Python 3.10 or later. The uv tool installs Python for you. On macOS, brew needs Homebrew: https://brew.sh. Open a new terminal after the install.

os.mac:
brew install uv
uv tool install multicloud-cli
uv tool update-shell
mctl --version
os.linux:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source "$HOME/.local/bin/env"
uv tool install multicloud-cli
uv tool update-shell
mctl --version
os.win:
# In the Ubuntu window
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source "$HOME/.local/bin/env"
uv tool install multicloud-cli
uv tool update-shell
mctl --version

steps.d: The output of aws --version must start with aws-cli/2.

os.linux:
sudo apt install -y unzip
curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o awscliv2.zip
unzip -q -o awscliv2.zip && sudo ./aws/install --update && rm -rf awscliv2.zip aws
aws --version
os.win:
# In the Ubuntu window
sudo apt install -y unzip        # or: sudo dnf install -y unzip
curl "https://awscli.amazonaws.com/awscli-exe-linux-x86_64.zip" -o awscliv2.zip
unzip -q -o awscliv2.zip && sudo ./aws/install --update && rm -rf awscliv2.zip aws
aws --version

steps.g: Fedora or RHEL: use sudo dnf install -y unzip. ARM Linux (uname -m prints aarch64): use awscli-exe-linux-aarch64.zip.

steps.d: OpenTofu creates the Multicloud role in your AWS account. Terraform 1.10 or later also works.

os.linux:
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://get.opentofu.org/install-opentofu.sh -o install-opentofu.sh
chmod +x install-opentofu.sh && ./install-opentofu.sh --install-method standalone
rm install-opentofu.sh && tofu version
os.win:
# In the Ubuntu window
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL https://get.opentofu.org/install-opentofu.sh -o install-opentofu.sh
chmod +x install-opentofu.sh && ./install-opentofu.sh --install-method standalone
rm install-opentofu.sh && tofu version

steps.d: You need them from the stage “Prepare your cluster” on. The connector needs helm 3.14 or later.

os.mac:
brew install kubectl helm jq
kubectl version --client && helm version
os.linux:
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -Ls https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
sudo install -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl && rm kubectl
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
sudo apt install -y jq
kubectl version --client && helm version
os.win:
# In the Ubuntu window
curl -LO "https://dl.k8s.io/release/$(curl -Ls https://dl.k8s.io/release/stable.txt)/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl"
sudo install -m 0755 kubectl /usr/local/bin/kubectl && rm kubectl
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
sudo apt install -y jq
kubectl version --client && helm version

steps.g: Fedora or RHEL: use sudo dnf install -y jq. ARM Linux (uname -m prints aarch64): replace linux/amd64 with linux/arm64 in the kubectl URL.
